## Interventions and optimization — Day 2, Session 4

Worksheet: `worksheets/08-interventions-and-optimization.qmd`. The
chapter is [Interventions and
optimization](../chapters/15-interventions-and-optimization.qmd).

The state vector carries a fourth component $C$, cumulative incidence, so a
question about the whole epidemic becomes a single number to read off. $C(T)$
counts the infections generated after $t = 0$ and up to the horizon $T$; it
excludes the ten people already infectious, and it is not the eventual epidemic
total unless transmission has finished. Parameters travel as a plain vector
because the callback mutates entry 4 in place, and a `NamedTuple` is immutable.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch15-setup
using CairoMakie
using DiffEqCallbacks
using EpiModelingCourse
using Optimization
using OptimizationOptimJL
using OrdinaryDiffEq

check(name, condition) =
    println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint")

baseline = BASELINE_PARAMETERS
u0 = Float64[990.0, 10.0, 0.0, 0.0]        # S, I, R, C
time_grid = collect(0.0:0.1:45.0)
intervention_duration = 10.0
maximum_reduction = 0.5

function policy_sir!(du, u, p, t)
    β, c, γ, reduction, N = p
    S, I, R, C = u
    incidence = β * c * (1 - reduction) * S * I / N
    du[1] = -incidence
    du[2] = incidence - γ * I
    du[3] = γ * I
    du[4] = incidence
    return nothing
end

println("R₀ = ", baseline.beta * baseline.contact_rate / baseline.gamma)
```

### Part A — one policy, written out

`PresetTimeCallback` stops the integrator at the named times and runs `affect!`,
which flips the reduction on and back off. The condition is
`integrator.t < stop_time` rather than `== start_time`, so one closure handles
both scheduled times.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch15-a1
function run_scenario(
    start_time;
    duration = intervention_duration,
    reduction = maximum_reduction,
    horizon = last(time_grid),
)
    stop_time = start_time + duration
    initial_reduction = start_time <= 0.0 < stop_time ? reduction : 0.0
    parameters = [
        baseline.beta,           # 1: β
        baseline.contact_rate,   # 2: c
        baseline.gamma,          # 3: γ
        initial_reduction,       # 4: the policy — this is the one that moves
        baseline.N,              # 5: N
    ]
    function affect!(integrator)
        integrator.p[4] = integrator.t < stop_time ? reduction : 0.0
        return nothing
    end
    callback = PresetTimeCallback(unique([start_time, stop_time]), affect!)
    problem = ODEProblem(policy_sir!, u0, (0.0, horizon), parameters)
    return solve(problem, Tsit5(); callback = callback,
                 saveat = 0.0:0.1:horizon, abstol = 1e-8, reltol = 1e-8)
end

no_intervention = solve(
    ODEProblem(policy_sir!, u0, (0.0, last(time_grid)),
               [baseline.beta, baseline.contact_rate, baseline.gamma, 0.0, baseline.N]),
    Tsit5(); saveat = time_grid, abstol = 1e-8, reltol = 1e-8)

reference_start = 8.0
reference_solution = run_scenario(reference_start)

baseline_array = Array(no_intervention)
# A callback forces extra saved points, so interpolate back onto the grid.
reference_array = Array(reference_solution(time_grid))

check("S + I + R is conserved",
      maximum(abs.(vec(sum(reference_array[1:3, :]; dims = 1)) .- baseline.N)) < 1e-6)
check("a zero-length policy is the same as no policy",
      Array(run_scenario(0.0; duration = 0.0))[4, end] ≈ baseline_array[4, end])

(; incidence_none = round(baseline_array[4, end]; digits = 2),
   incidence_reference = round(reference_array[4, end]; digits = 2),
   difference_at_45 = round(baseline_array[4, end] - reference_array[4, end]; digits = 2))
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch15-scenario
#| fig-cap: "A ten-unit, 50% reduction starting at t = 8 compared with no intervention. The shaded band is the policy window; the second rise after it lifts is a rebound, not a numerical artifact."
fig = Figure(size = (860, 420))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time", ylabel = "infectious people")
vspan!(ax, reference_start, reference_start + intervention_duration;
       color = (:grey, 0.2))
lines!(ax, time_grid, baseline_array[2, :]; color = :firebrick, label = "none")
lines!(ax, time_grid, reference_array[2, :]; color = :seagreen,
       label = "50% for 10 units from t = 8")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch15-a2
susceptibles_when_policy_lifts =
    reference_solution(reference_start + intervention_duration)[1]

long_none = Array(solve(
    ODEProblem(policy_sir!, u0, (0.0, 200.0),
               [baseline.beta, baseline.contact_rate, baseline.gamma, 0.0, baseline.N]),
    Tsit5(); saveat = 0.0:0.1:200.0, abstol = 1e-8, reltol = 1e-8))
long_reference = Array(run_scenario(reference_start; horizon = 200.0))

difference_at_45 = baseline_array[4, end] - reference_array[4, end]
difference_at_200 = long_none[4, end] - long_reference[4, end]

check("the long-horizon benefit is smaller than the T = 45 benefit",
      difference_at_200 < difference_at_45)

(; susceptibles_when_policy_lifts = round(susceptibles_when_policy_lifts; digits = 1),
   R_eff_when_policy_lifts =
       round(baseline.beta * baseline.contact_rate / baseline.gamma *
             susceptibles_when_policy_lifts / baseline.N; digits = 3),
   difference_at_45 = round(difference_at_45; digits = 2),
   difference_at_200 = round(difference_at_200; digits = 2),
   postponed_beyond_45 = round(difference_at_45 - difference_at_200; digits = 2))
```

#### A1. Interpret

- The intervention postpones most of the epidemic rather than ending it. Inside
  the window $C$ still climbs by about 104, against about 400 over the same
  interval with no policy.
- When the window lifts at $t = 18$ there are still about 778 susceptibles, far
  above the herd-immunity threshold $S^{*} = N/R_0 = 500$, so
  $R_{\text{eff}} \approx 1.56$ and the epidemic restarts. It peaks a second time
  at about 96 around $t = 30$, later and lower than the untouched peak of 158 at
  $t = 17.5$. The policy protected the susceptible pool rather than depleting it,
  which is exactly why the rebound is available.
- The bookkeeping is where the lesson is. By $t = 45$, 785 people have been
  infected without the policy and 695 with it, a difference of about 91. Run the
  same comparison to $t = 200$, by which point both epidemics have finished, and
  the difference is only about 51 — roughly 40 of those 91 cases were pushed past
  the horizon rather than prevented.
- Three impressions are available from one run: the suppressed first peak looks
  like near-total success, $T = 45$ gives 91, and $T = 200$ gives 51. None is
  wrong. What would be wrong is quoting any of them without saying which horizon
  it belongs to, because "91 infections averted" will be heard as prevention.
- A policy that ends while the population is still largely susceptible buys time
  rather than immunity, and what the time is worth is a judgement the model does
  not contain.

### Part B — the objective landscape

Nothing about the model changes; what changes is that we are prepared to run it
many times and compare. The grid is a diagnostic, not the method.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch15-b1
function incidence_at_horizon(x, _)
    solution = run_scenario(x[1])
    return Array(solution)[4, end]
end

candidate_starts = collect(0.0:0.25:25.0)
horizon_curve = [incidence_at_horizon([s], nothing) for s in candidate_starts]

check("it agrees with the Part A scenario",
      incidence_at_horizon([reference_start], nothing) ≈ reference_array[4, end])

(; grid_best_start = candidate_starts[argmin(horizon_curve)],
   grid_best_value = round(minimum(horizon_curve); digits = 2))
```

`Fminbox(LBFGS())` is a *local* method, so "it converged" is not the same as "it
found the best point in the box". Check the retcode, the position and the value
separately.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch15-b2
incidence_problem = OptimizationProblem(
    OptimizationFunction(incidence_at_horizon, AutoFiniteDiff()),
    [reference_start], nothing; lb = [0.0], ub = [25.0])
incidence_solution = solve(incidence_problem, Fminbox(LBFGS()); maxiters = 30)

# incidence_start refers to the day the intervention switches on.
incidence_start = incidence_solution.u[1]

check("the solver reported success", successful_retcode(incidence_solution))
check("the optimizer agrees with the grid on where",
      abs(incidence_start - candidate_starts[argmin(horizon_curve)]) < 0.5)
check("the optimizer agrees with the grid on how good",
      abs(incidence_solution.objective - minimum(horizon_curve)) < 1.0)

(; incidence_start = round(incidence_start; digits = 3),
   incidence_value = round(incidence_solution.objective; digits = 2))
```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch15-b3
baseline_incidence_rate =
    baseline.beta * baseline.contact_rate .*
    baseline_array[1, :] .* baseline_array[2, :] ./ baseline.N

incidence_peak_time = time_grid[argmax(baseline_incidence_rate)]
prevalence_peak_time = time_grid[argmax(baseline_array[2, :])]

check("incidence peaks before prevalence does",
      incidence_peak_time < prevalence_peak_time)

(; incidence_peak_time, prevalence_peak_time,
   optimal_start = round(incidence_start; digits = 2))
```

#### B1. Interpret

- The curve is U-shaped with a minimum at $t_1 \approx 13.8$, where
  $C(45) \approx 638$ against 785 with no policy. Both figures are horizon-bound:
  at $T = 200$ the same two policies give about 680 and 790, so the gap narrows
  from 147 to 110.
- Both ends are bad for opposite reasons. Starting at $t_1 = 0$ spends the window
  while there is almost nothing to suppress, and the epidemic then runs its course
  from a nearly untouched susceptible pool, giving 756. Starting at $t_1 = 25$
  suppresses a tail that was going to fade anyway, giving 737.
- "Act at the peak" is ambiguous, because there are two peaks three units apart.
  Prevalence peaks at $t = 17.5$, but susceptible depletion runs at the incidence
  rate $\beta c SI/N$, which peaks at about $t = 14.3$ because $S$ is already
  falling while $I$ is still rising. The optimum at 13.8 is essentially *at* the
  peak that matters.
- What a fixed window is worth is how much depletion it prevents, so the best
  window is the one covering the interval of fastest depletion.
- The window does not carry the population through the threshold: $S$ is still
  about 532 when it closes, and 500 is not reached until about $t = 26.3$. What
  the policy buys is a smaller *overshoot* — transmission is still supercritical
  at the close, but with fewer infectious people to drive it, so the epidemic
  crosses the threshold with less momentum. By $t = 200$ about 310 susceptibles
  remain under the optimal policy against about 200 with none.
- "Act slightly before the peak" gets the right answer for the wrong reason; "act
  across the incidence peak, to cut the overshoot" generalizes. Note the shape is
  a consequence of holding duration and strength fixed — a policy that could be
  extended indefinitely would have no interior optimum at all.

### Part C — a different objective, a different answer

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch15-c1
function peak_prevalence(x, _)
    solution = run_scenario(x[1])
    return maximum(Array(solution)[2, :])
end

peak_curve = [peak_prevalence([s], nothing) for s in candidate_starts]

peak_problem = OptimizationProblem(
    OptimizationFunction(peak_prevalence, AutoFiniteDiff()),
    [reference_start], nothing; lb = [0.0], ub = [25.0])
peak_solution = solve(peak_problem, Fminbox(LBFGS()); maxiters = 30)
peak_start = peak_solution.u[1]

check("the two objectives disagree about when to act",
      abs(peak_start - incidence_start) > 2.0)

(; peak_start = round(peak_start; digits = 3),
   peak_value = round(peak_solution.objective; digits = 2),
   incidence_start = round(incidence_start; digits = 3))
```

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch15-c2
(
    no_policy = (peak = round(maximum(baseline_array[2, :]); digits = 1),
                 C45 = round(baseline_array[4, end]; digits = 1)),
    min_incidence = (peak = round(peak_prevalence([incidence_start], nothing); digits = 1),
                     C45 = round(incidence_at_horizon([incidence_start], nothing); digits = 1)),
    min_peak = (peak = round(peak_prevalence([peak_start], nothing); digits = 1),
                C45 = round(incidence_at_horizon([peak_start], nothing); digits = 1)),
)
```

The peak objective has a flat region, and a gradient method cannot see out of
one. The same optimisation is started from four different guesses; two of them
fail, and nothing in the result announces it.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch15-c3
function optimize_peak_from(guess)
    problem = OptimizationProblem(
        OptimizationFunction(peak_prevalence, AutoFiniteDiff()),
        [guess], nothing; lb = [0.0], ub = [25.0])
    solution = solve(problem, Fminbox(LBFGS()); maxiters = 30)
    return (guess = guess, start = round(solution.u[1]; digits = 3),
            value = round(solution.objective; digits = 2),
            converged = successful_retcode(solution))
end

attempts = [optimize_peak_from(g) for g in (8.0, 15.0, 20.0, 24.0)]

plateau_starts = candidate_starts[peak_curve .>= maximum(baseline_array[2, :]) - 1e-6]
plateau_begins = isempty(plateau_starts) ? 25.0 : minimum(plateau_starts)

check("a late starting guess does not move at all",
      abs(attempts[3].start - 20.0) < 0.01 && abs(attempts[4].start - 24.0) < 0.01)
check("every attempt reports success, including the stuck ones",
      all(a -> a.converged, attempts))

(; attempts, plateau_begins)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch15-objectives
#| fig-cap: "Two objectives over the same decision variable. The minima fall four time units apart, and the peak objective is exactly flat once the window opens after the untouched peak at t = 17.5 — the shaded region, where a gradient optimizer stops immediately."
fig = Figure(size = (860, 640))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; ylabel = "C(45), cumulative incidence at t = 45",
           title = "Same model, same decision variable, two objectives")
lines!(ax1, candidate_starts, horizon_curve; color = :darkorange, linewidth = 2)
scatter!(ax1, [incidence_start], [incidence_solution.objective];
         color = :firebrick, markersize = 14)
vlines!(ax1, [incidence_start]; color = :firebrick, linestyle = :dash)

ax2 = Axis(fig[2, 1]; xlabel = "intervention start time t₁",
           ylabel = "peak infectious people")
vspan!(ax2, plateau_begins, 25.0; color = (:grey, 0.2))
lines!(ax2, candidate_starts, peak_curve; color = :seagreen, linewidth = 2)
scatter!(ax2, [peak_start], [peak_solution.objective];
         color = :firebrick, markersize = 14)
vlines!(ax2, [incidence_start]; color = :firebrick, linestyle = :dash)
text!(ax2, 19.0, 120.0; text = "flat: gradient = 0", fontsize = 13)
linkxaxes!(ax1, ax2)
fig
```

#### C1. Interpret

- The two objectives disagree, and not marginally: minimising $C(45)$ says start
  at $t_1 \approx 13.8$, minimising the peak says $t_1 \approx 9.6$. Minimising
  the peak nearly halves it, 158 down to 80, at a price of about 35 more
  infections by $t = 45$; minimising $C(45)$ lowers it by 147 while leaving the
  peak at 137, barely 13% below doing nothing.
- Neither is the right answer, because "optimal" is not a property of the
  epidemic. It is a property of the objective, which encodes a value judgement
  about whether horizon-specific burden or peak demand is the thing to avoid. A
  hospital with a hard bed ceiling should act earlier than a planner counting
  infections by day 45, and both are optimising correctly.
- Writing the objective down explicitly, as the four-piece assembly forces you to,
  is what makes that judgement auditable instead of buried.
- Starting the peak optimisation from $t_1 = 8$ or $15$ finds 9.6; starting from
  20 or 24 returns the guess unchanged with a "converged" peak of 158.45 —
  exactly the no-intervention peak, because a window opening after $t = 17.5$
  cannot touch a maximum that has already occurred. The objective is constant
  there, the finite-difference gradient is zero, and LBFGS correctly concludes it
  is at a stationary point.
- Every diagnostic looks healthy: converged, inside the box, plausible number.
  Only comparing against the grid reveals the answer is 97% worse than the real
  optimum. Retcodes tell you the solver finished cleanly, not that it finished
  anywhere useful.
- The lesson is not "grid search everything", which does not scale past two or
  three decision variables. It is that a gradient method assumes a locally
  informative slope, and that assumption should be checked: sweep the objective in
  one dimension when you can, restart from several guesses when you cannot, and be
  suspicious of an optimizer that returns its own starting point. Here the flat
  region even has a mechanistic explanation — it begins at the untouched peak
  time, which you can predict before running anything.
